extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic and philosophy (undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the nature, structure, and justificatory force of induction and the syllogism, with formal requirements for valid syllogistic argument and philosophical critique of popular doctrines about universals and propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as a real process of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a process of real inference: the conclusion of an induction 'embraces more than is contained in the premises.' A principle ascertained by experience is more than a mere summing up of observed cases; it is a generalization expressive of the belief that what was true in observed cases is true in an indefinite number of unobserved cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive conclusions extend beyond particular observations to unobserved (even future) cases. Conditions necessary to make induction legitimate are noted as important and deferred to further discussion (Third Book). Example: forming a general proposition from many observed instances and using it to infer about unobserved instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential structure of a legitimate syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate syllogism must contain three, and no more than three, propositions (a conclusion and two premises) and three, and no more than three, terms (the subject and predicate of the conclusion and a middle term present in both premises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify major, minor, and middle terms; the premise containing the middle and major term is the major premise, the one with the middle and minor is the minor premise. Validity depends on these structural constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and moods determine legitimate syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are classified into figures (by position of the middle term) and moods (by quantity and quality — universal/particular, affirmative/negative). Only certain combinations (moods) in each figure are legitimate — examples of all legitimate moods are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the exemplars/blank forms provided (first through fourth figures and their legitimate moods) as templates for constructing valid syllogisms. Singular propositions are treated with universals for syllogistic purposes (e.g., 'Socrates is a man' counts with universal form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to the first figure (rules for reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every valid ratiocination can be expressed in first-figure forms; arguments in other figures can be reduced to the first figure by conversion of one or both premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply simple conversion for universal negatives and conversion per accidens for universal affirmatives when necessary. Examples: No C is B + All A is B => No A is C after conversion; All B is A may be converted per accidens to Some A is B to obtain a first-figure form. Note: some arguments may be more naturally expressed in other figures even though reducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major premise must be universal; minor premise affirmative
rubrics_metrics.description: In the two general first-figure formulæ, the major premise is a universal proposition, and the other premise (the minor) is always affirmative; the conclusion's quality corresponds to the major premise's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating syllogisms, ensure the major premise is expressed as a universal (affirmative or negative) and the minor affirms inclusion of subject in the class named by the major. This determines whether the conclusion will be affirmative or negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions must convey factual content, not only classificatory/linguistic relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition that merely expresses the meaning of words (a verbal or classificatory account) is insufficient; true propositions assert matters of fact dependent on laws of nature, not mere conventions of naming or classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate premises for substantive factual import (attributes and their co-occurrence) rather than treating them as mere definitions or name manipulations. The critique targets views (Hobbes, Condillac, nominalists) that reduce propositions to language alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying factual axioms of syllogistic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Two fundamental principles ground the probative force of syllogisms: (1) Affirmative: things which co-exist with the same thing co-exist with one another (transitivity of coexistence). (2) Negative: a thing which co-exists with another thing, with which a third thing does not co-exist, is not co-existent with that third thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity of syllogistic moves should be traced to these factual axioms rather than to mere logical convention. Use these as criteria to judge whether premises legitimately support the conclusion (i.e., they concern real relations of attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism as mark/evidence formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every syllogism can be phrased as: 'Attribute A is a mark of attribute B; the given object has mark A; therefore the object has attribute B.' General propositions function as marks enabling practical inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an argument's practical application, recast general premises as marks/evidence for other attributes. This phraseology clarifies how syllogisms operate in practice and unifies affirmative/negative axioms into 'whatever has any mark has that which it is a mark of.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular propositions treated as universal in syllogistic use
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular propositions are ranked with universal propositions for syllogistic purposes because their predicate is affirmed or denied of the whole of the subject (e.g., 'Socrates is a man' functions like a universal assertion for form purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat statements about individuals as if they were universal for the purpose of placing them into syllogistic moods/figures; this explains why certain singular examples fit standard moods of the first figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: The syllogism does not originate new inference beyond the content of premises; distinguish inferring from recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Though syllogisms display conclusions that may seem new to a hearer, the actual inferential work resides in the prior generalization (induction) from observed instances. The syllogism often functions as a register or decoding of already-completed inferences rather than producing the inference itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating an argument's epistemic origin, trace general premises back to their inductive origin in observation. Beware attributing the generation of new knowledge to mere deductive restatement of an already-held generalization (the distinction between inferring and registering one's notes).
